# **He et al. (2016):** Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

## Deeper nets fit the <em>training</em> set worse; an identity shortcut — free wherever shapes match — reverses that and takes **3.57%** top-5

<p class="byline"><strong>He, Zhang, Ren &amp; Sun</strong> · Microsoft Research · CVPR 2016, arXiv Dec 2015</p>

<p class="links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385">arXiv</a><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.03385v1">PDF</a><a href="https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_cvpr_2016/html/He_Deep_Residual_Learning_CVPR_2016_paper.html">CVPR open access</a><a href="https://github.com/KaimingHe/deep-residual-networks">code</a><a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385">section anchors</a></p>

<p class="byline"><em>Underlines in review mode are fact-checked against the paper — hover one to open the explanation.</em></p>

---

<a class="slide-id" id="0ab4f673-ad0d-4e82-bb77-81bf0dc5eca6"></a>

## TL;DR

- **What it is** — a wiring rule: every few layers get an **identity shortcut** carrying their input around them.
- **The trick** — a block computes `y = F(x) + x`, so the layers fit the **residual**; **doing nothing means driving F to zero**, which leaves the block close to an identity.
- **A fair test** — the identity shortcut adds **no parameters**, so a residual net and its **plain twin** — the same VGG-style conv stack (Table 1), shortcuts removed — match on **depth, width, parameters and FLOPs** (multiply-adds per image). The deeper production nets add a **1x1 projection only between stages** ([slide 13](#13)); a **stage** is a run of blocks at one feature-map size, and at each stage boundary the design halves the map and doubles the channels.
- **The numbers** — the reversal, in top-1 error (%): **plain-34 worse than plain-18** (28.54 vs 27.94 top-1), **ResNet-34 better than ResNet-18** (25.03 vs 27.88); an ensemble of six reaches **3.57%** <span class="term" data-tiphead="Top-5 error" data-tip="The share of test images whose true class is not among the model's five highest-scoring classes. Top-1 error counts an image as wrong whenever the single best guess is wrong.">top-5 error</span> and wins <span class="term" data-tiphead="ILSVRC" data-tip="The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, the yearly competition on the ImageNet benchmark. Its classification track ranks entries by top-5 error on a held-out test set scored by the organisers' server.">ILSVRC 2015</span>.
- **Why it mattered** — residual connections went **universal**, transformers included; the *why* never settled.

*Both numbers are top-5 error on the same 1000-class task. The headline **3.57%** is an **ensemble of six models** of different depth — the paper does not say how their outputs are combined — scored on the test set and took **1st place at ILSVRC 2015**; the best **single** model — **ResNet-152**, 152 layers, **11.3 billion FLOPs** — is **4.49%** on validation (Tables 4 and 5, p. 6).*

## The core idea — ask the layers for the correction, not the answer

<div class="columns-wide-left">
<div>

- **Why care:** **more layers made the network worse on its own training set**.
- **What prior work does:** [batch normalisation (BN)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167) and <span class="term" data-tiphead="Normalized initialisation" data-tip="Background: drawing each layer's initial weights with a variance scaled to its number of inputs, so activations neither shrink nor blow up from layer to layer at the start of training. This paper initialises its weights as in He et al. 2015.">normalized initialisation</span> had largely solved **convergence**, meaning here that a deep net *starts* to train: its loss falls instead of stalling from the first iterations. The paper argues the remaining failure is therefore not signal propagation, and backs that on [slide 18](#18).
- **What this paper does instead:** the block computes `H(x) = F(x) + x`, so layers learn only **the correction**.
- **The enabling fact:** a deeper net can **copy a shallower one and pad with identity layers** — a good solution **provably exists**.
- **Closest relative:** the concurrent [highway networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.00387) gate their shortcuts with learned, data-dependent weights; this one is **ungated and parameter-free**.

</div>
<div>

<figure class="credit"><img src="images/paper/fig2-block.png" width="340" data-tiphead="Figure 2 — the building block" data-tip="The paper's own drawing of one residual block: two weight layers compute F(x), the curved identity path carries x around them, and the two are added before the final ReLU. Slide 11 redraws it piece by piece."/><figcaption>Figure 2 from <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385">He et al. 2016</a>, p. 2</figcaption></figure>

</div>
</div>

## The five Cs, in one look

Five Cs — a standard first-pass checklist for a paper: Category, Context, Correctness, Contributions, Clarity.

- **Category** — an **empirical architecture paper**: one wiring change, defended by ablations on two datasets.
- **Context** — [VGG](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.1556) and [GoogLeNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.4842) (depth by hand), [batch norm](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167) (convergence, assumed here), [highway nets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.00387) (gated shortcuts, no demonstrated gain past 100 layers).
- **Correctness** — one construction plus **matched-parameter comparisons**; both hold. *Why* residuals are easier to fit stays a **hypothesis**.
- **Contributions** — degradation as a **training-error** result; the identity shortcut; the **bottleneck** block; five 1st places — ILSVRC 2015 classification, ImageNet detection and localization, COCO detection and segmentation.
- **Clarity** — very high: Figures 1, 2 and 5 carry the argument, and the authors state their own negative results.

<a class="slide-id" id="b3c3df89-7a35-4161-b6ab-58c601edff2b"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-lg -->

## Should you read further?

- **Read the introduction and §4.1, the ImageNet experiments, if** you design or debug deep stacks — the reasoning that turns *"it got worse"* into a **falsifiable diagnosis** is the transferable part; the deck walks it on slides 7–10 and 16–18.
- **Read §3, the method — residual learning, the shortcut, the network designs — with Figures 1, 2 and 5 if** you want just the mechanism: the **construction argument**, the block, and the shortcut options. That is the whole mechanism, on slides 10–15.
- **Skip it if** you want to know *why* residuals help: this paper does not answer that (slides 18–19). Go to [ensembles of shallow paths](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.06431), [shattered gradients](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08591) or [loss-surface visualisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.09913) instead.

<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Why this is not overfitting" data-tip="Overfitting means the model fits the training set too well and the test set worse. Here the deeper model fits the training set worse. Nothing about capacity or regularisation can explain a higher training error.">
<rect x="40" y="410" width="1080" height="170" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="66" y="442" class="degr-t" font-size="16">Read the left panel first, and the argument is finished before the right panel starts</text>
<text x="66" y="472" class="degr-d" font-size="13.5">An overfitting model drives TRAINING error down and TEST error up. The 56-layer plain net does the opposite: it is worse on the</text>
<text x="66" y="496" class="degr-d" font-size="13.5">data it is being optimised on. More data, more augmentation and more regularisation are all answers to a problem this net does</text>
<text x="66" y="520" class="degr-d" font-size="13.5">not have. The paper's word for it is degradation, and it calls the effect unexpected and not caused by overfitting.</text>
<text x="66" y="552" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Redrawn from Figure 1 (CIFAR-10). Curve shapes are schematic; the paper prints no endpoint values on this figure.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>
</div>

- The <span class="term" data-tiphead="The degradation problem" data-tip="With the network depth increasing, accuracy gets saturated and then degrades rapidly. The paper's point is that this shows up first as higher training error, which is why it cannot be overfitting.">degradation problem</span>: accuracy saturates, then **degrades rapidly** — and the paper says it is **not caused by overfitting**
- This panel is [CIFAR-10](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar.html); the same effect appears on ImageNet at 18 and 34 layers — [slide 16](#16)
- **One recipe for every depth**, not tuned per net: learning rate 0.1, divided by 10 at 32k and 48k iterations, stop at 64k (§4.2). On ImageNet, 3x the iterations did not close the gap either ([slide 18](#18))

<a class="slide-id" id="c64d3e0f-6c0f-4bea-ae15-8c14f759e7a1"></a>

## Three failures look alike from a distance, and the paper is only about the third

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.4rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="980" height="507" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.thre-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.thre-d{fill:#a0a0a0}.thre-ax{fill:#6e6e6e;font-size:11}.thre-v{fill:#8a8a8a;font-size:12}</style>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="40" y="38" class="thre-t" font-size="17">One symptom on a loss curve, three different diagnoses — and three different fixes</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Overfitting" data-tip="The model memorises the training set. Training error keeps falling, held-out error turns back up, and the gap between them widens. This is the failure ResNet is NOT about.">
<rect x="40" y="58" width="345" height="512" rx="12" fill="#151515" stroke="#4a3520" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="64" y="92" fill="#f0883e" font-size="16" font-weight="700">1. Overfitting</text>
<text x="64" y="114" class="thre-v">too much capacity for the data</text>
<text x="64" y="330" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="12.5">Training error keeps falling, held-out</text>
<text x="64" y="352" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="12.5">error turns back up. The gap is it.</text>
<text x="64" y="374" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">Fix: more data, augmentation, dropout.</text>
<text x="64" y="440" fill="#f0883e" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700">Not what Figure 1 shows.</text>
<text x="64" y="466" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">Figure 1 has the deeper net WORSE on</text>
<text x="64" y="488" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">training data. No amount of regularising</text>
<text x="64" y="510" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">fixes a model that underfits.</text>
</a>
<path d="M72,160 L72,285 L352,285" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/>
<path d="M72,172 L140,214 L200,242 L260,260 L352,272" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none"/>
<path d="M72,178 L140,208 L200,222 L260,216 L352,198" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none"/>
<text x="356" y="276" fill="#3fb950" font-size="11">train</text>
<text x="356" y="202" fill="#f0883e" font-size="11">test</text>
<text x="212" y="306" text-anchor="middle" class="thre-ax">iterations, error on the y axis</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Vanishing or exploding gradients" data-tip="The signal dies on its way through the stack and the network never starts converging. The paper's introduction says this had been largely addressed by normalized initialization and intermediate normalization layers.">
<rect x="407" y="58" width="345" height="512" rx="12" fill="#151515" stroke="#3a3a55" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="431" y="92" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="16" font-weight="700">2. Vanishing gradients</text>
<text x="431" y="114" class="thre-v">the signal dies on the way through</text>
<text x="431" y="330" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="12.5">The net never starts converging at all.</text>
<text x="431" y="352" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">Fix: normalized init and BN. The intro</text>
<text x="431" y="374" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">calls this largely addressed already.</text>
<text x="431" y="440" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700">Largely solved before this paper.</text>
<text x="431" y="466" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">Every plain and residual net here is</text>
<text x="431" y="488" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">trained with batch normalisation, and</text>
<text x="431" y="510" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">all of them converge. See slide 18.</text>
</a>
<path d="M439,160 L439,285 L719,285" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/>
<path d="M439,174 L500,171 L560,173 L640,170 L719,172" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none"/>
<text x="579" y="200" text-anchor="middle" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="11">error never moves</text>
<text x="579" y="306" text-anchor="middle" class="thre-ax">iterations, error on the y axis</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Degradation" data-tip="The network converges perfectly happily, and still lands at a higher training error than a shallower version of itself. This is the failure the paper isolates and the one residual learning is aimed at.">
<rect x="774" y="58" width="345" height="512" rx="12" fill="#151515" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="798" y="92" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="16" font-weight="700">3. Degradation</text>
<text x="798" y="114" class="thre-v">converges fine, converges worse</text>
<text x="798" y="330" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="12.5">The net converges, but the deeper one</text>
<text x="798" y="352" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="12.5">lands at HIGHER training error.</text>
<text x="798" y="374" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">Fix: nobody had one. Hence this paper.</text>
<text x="798" y="440" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700">This is the paper's target.</text>
<text x="798" y="466" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">Saturation with depth might be dull.</text>
<text x="798" y="488" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">Getting rapidly worse while the solver</text>
<text x="798" y="510" class="thre-d" font-size="12.5">is still working is not.</text>
</a>
<path d="M806,160 L806,285 L1086,285" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/>
<path d="M806,172 L860,220 L920,246 L1000,262 L1086,270" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none"/>
<path d="M806,172 L860,202 L920,220 L1000,232 L1086,238" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none"/>
<text x="1090" y="274" fill="#3fb950" font-size="11">20</text>
<text x="1090" y="242" fill="#f0883e" font-size="11">56</text>
<text x="946" y="306" text-anchor="middle" class="thre-ax">both curves are TRAINING error</text>
</svg>
</div>

<a class="slide-id" id="f868eecd-0848-44b1-bde4-06dafa13e8c3"></a>

## A deeper net can copy a shallower one and pad with identity layers — so the obstacle is the search, not the model

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.4rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="980" height="507" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.cons-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.cons-d{fill:#a0a0a0}.cons-lb{fill:#7a7a7a;font-size:12}.cons-s1{animation:cons-s1 9s linear infinite}.cons-s2{animation:cons-s2 9s linear infinite}.cons-s3{animation:cons-s3 9s linear infinite}.cons-s4{animation:cons-s4 9s linear infinite}.cons-s5{animation:cons-s5 9s linear infinite}.cons-s6{animation:cons-s6 9s linear infinite}.cons-s7{animation:cons-s7 9s linear infinite}.cons-s8{animation:cons-s8 9s linear infinite}.cons-s9{animation:cons-s9 9s linear infinite}@keyframes cons-s1{0%,2%{opacity:0.25}6%{opacity:1}100%{opacity:1}}@keyframes cons-s2{0%,8%{opacity:0.25}12%{opacity:1}100%{opacity:1}}@keyframes cons-s3{0%,14%{opacity:0.25}18%{opacity:1}100%{opacity:1}}@keyframes cons-s4{0%,26%{opacity:0.25}30%{opacity:1}100%{opacity:1}}@keyframes cons-s5{0%,32%{opacity:0.25}36%{opacity:1}100%{opacity:1}}@keyframes cons-s6{0%,38%{opacity:0.25}42%{opacity:1}100%{opacity:1}}@keyframes cons-s7{0%,48%{opacity:0.25}52%{opacity:1}100%{opacity:1}}@keyframes cons-s8{0%,62%{opacity:0.4}66%{opacity:1}100%{opacity:1}}@keyframes cons-s9{0%,78%{opacity:0.4}82%{opacity:1}100%{opacity:1}}</style>
<defs>
<marker id="cg" markerWidth="11" markerHeight="11" refX="8" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4 L0,8 z" fill="#3b82f6"/></marker>
</defs>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="40" y="36" class="cons-t" font-size="17">The constructed solution, drawn — and the reason it stays theoretical</text>
<text x="80" y="76" fill="#3fb950" font-size="13.5" font-weight="700">shallower net</text>
<g data-tiphead="A trained shallower network" data-tip="Take any network that has already been trained to some training error. Call that error E.">
<rect x="80" y="88" width="170" height="42" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="165" y="114" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">learned layer</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="A trained shallower network" data-tip="Nothing special about these layers: they are whatever the shallower model happened to converge to.">
<rect x="80" y="138" width="170" height="42" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="165" y="164" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">learned layer</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="A trained shallower network" data-tip="The stack is drawn with three layers only for the picture; the argument holds for any depth.">
<rect x="80" y="188" width="170" height="42" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="165" y="214" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">learned layer</text>
</g>
<text x="165" y="258" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3fb950" font-size="13" font-weight="700">training error E</text>
<path d="M256,175 L324,175" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none" marker-end="url(#cg)"/>
<text x="330" y="76" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="13.5" font-weight="700">deeper counterpart</text>
<g class="cons-s1" opacity="1" data-tiphead="The copied layers" data-tip="The first layers of the deeper model are copied verbatim from the learned shallower model. Nothing is retrained.">
<rect x="330" y="88" width="170" height="42" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="415" y="114" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">copied layer</text>
</g>
<g class="cons-s2" opacity="1" data-tiphead="The copied layers" data-tip="Same weights, same order. The deeper model starts out reproducing the shallower model exactly.">
<rect x="330" y="138" width="170" height="42" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="415" y="164" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">copied layer</text>
</g>
<g class="cons-s3" opacity="1" data-tiphead="The copied layers" data-tip="This is why the shallower model's solution space is a subspace of the deeper model's solution space.">
<rect x="330" y="188" width="170" height="42" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="415" y="214" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">copied layer</text>
</g>
<g class="cons-s4" opacity="1" data-tiphead="The added layers are identity" data-tip="Every extra layer just passes its input through unchanged, so the deeper network computes exactly the same function as the shallower one.">
<rect x="330" y="242" width="170" height="42" rx="8" fill="#10141a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
<text x="415" y="268" text-anchor="middle" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="13">identity layer</text>
</g>
<g class="cons-s5" opacity="1" data-tiphead="The added layers are identity" data-tip="Add as many of these as you like. None of them can raise the training error, because none of them changes the output.">
<rect x="330" y="292" width="170" height="42" rx="8" fill="#10141a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
<text x="415" y="318" text-anchor="middle" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="13">identity layer</text>
</g>
<g class="cons-s6" opacity="1" data-tiphead="The added layers are identity" data-tip="Fitting an identity mapping with a stack of nonlinear layers is exactly what the paper suspects solvers find hard. One illustrative way to build it: a 3x3 kernel with a single centred 1 for its own channel, BN set to undo its own normalisation, and a ReLU that sees only non-negative inputs because they come from the previous ReLU.">
<rect x="330" y="342" width="170" height="42" rx="8" fill="#10141a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
<text x="415" y="368" text-anchor="middle" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="13">identity layer</text>
</g>
<text class="cons-s7" opacity="1" x="415" y="412" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="13" font-weight="700">training error is still E</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="The constructed solution" data-tip="The paper: there exists a solution by construction to the deeper model, the added layers are identity mapping, and the other layers are copied from the learned shallower model.">
<rect x="560" y="60" width="560" height="180" rx="12" fill="#151515" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="586" y="94" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15.5" font-weight="700">What the construction proves</text>
<text x="586" y="126" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">A deeper model is at least as expressive: the shallower model's</text>
<text x="586" y="150" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">solution space is a subspace of the deeper model's. So a deeper</text>
<text x="586" y="174" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">model should produce no higher training error than its shallower</text>
<text x="586" y="198" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">counterpart. Representational capacity cannot be the obstacle,</text>
<text x="586" y="222" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">because the good solution provably exists inside the deeper net.</text>
</a>
<a class="cons-s8" opacity="1" href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="What experiments find" data-tip="The paper: experiments show that our current solvers on hand are unable to find solutions that are comparably good or better than the constructed solution, or unable to do so in feasible time.">
<rect x="560" y="258" width="560" height="150" rx="12" fill="#1a1113" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="586" y="292" fill="#f85149" font-size="15.5" font-weight="700">What actually happens</text>
<text x="586" y="324" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">SGD does not find that solution. The paper is careful about the</text>
<text x="586" y="348" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">wording: solvers are unable to find solutions comparably good or</text>
<text x="586" y="372" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">better than the constructed one, or unable to do so in feasible</text>
<text x="586" y="396" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">time. Note that this is a claim about search, not about capacity.</text>
</a>
<a class="cons-s9" opacity="1" href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Why this motivates residual learning" data-tip="If the useful thing is hard to reach because it sits near an identity mapping, change the parameterisation so that identity is what you get when the weights are zero.">
<rect x="40" y="446" width="1080" height="140" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="66" y="476" class="cons-t" font-size="16">The gap between those two boxes is the entire motivation for residual learning</text>
<text x="66" y="502" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">The good solution exists and the solver cannot reach it. The paper suspects solvers have difficulty approximating identity with</text>
<text x="66" y="524" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">several nonlinear layers. One way to see why (illustrative): conv, BN and ReLU copy their input only at one exact setting — a single</text>
<text x="66" y="546" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">centred 1 per channel in each 3x3 kernel, BN tuned to undo itself. The paper's response is to change the parameterisation instead,</text>
<text x="66" y="568" class="cons-d" font-size="13.5">so that identity becomes the easy default: drive the weights toward zero and the block passes its input through.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>

<text x="420" y="386" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="14.5" font-weight="700">F(x) — the residual function; every parameter of the block is in here</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S3.SS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Reading the block" data-tip="The block is defined in Section 3.2 of the paper as y = F(x, {Wi}) + x, where F is the residual mapping to be learned.">
<rect x="40" y="406" width="530" height="176" rx="12" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="64" y="438" class="bloc-t" font-size="15.5">Every piece, named</text>
<text x="64" y="468" class="bloc-d" font-size="13">x — the block input, and the thing the shortcut carries</text>
<text x="64" y="492" class="bloc-d" font-size="13">weight layer — a convolution with batch normalisation after it</text>
<text x="64" y="516" class="bloc-d" font-size="13">F(x) — what the two weight layers compute, biases omitted</text>
<text x="64" y="540" class="bloc-d" font-size="13">+ — element-wise addition of two feature maps, channel by channel</text>
<text x="64" y="564" class="bloc-d" font-size="13">the second ReLU is applied after the addition, not before it</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S3.SS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Why parameter-free matters" data-tip="Because the shortcut costs nothing, a plain net and a residual net can be built with identical depth, width, parameter count and FLOPs. Without that, the comparison in Table 2 would be confounded.">
<rect x="590" y="406" width="530" height="176" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="614" y="438" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15.5" font-weight="700">What the shortcut costs, and why that matters</text>
<text x="614" y="468" class="bloc-d" font-size="13">Parameters added: none — there is no matrix on the identity path.</text>
<text x="614" y="492" class="bloc-d" font-size="13">Computation added: one element-wise add per activation, which the</text>
<text x="614" y="516" class="bloc-d" font-size="13">paper calls negligible next to the convolutions.</text>
<text x="614" y="540" class="bloc-d" font-size="13">So plain and residual nets can be matched on depth, width, parameter</text>
<text x="614" y="564" class="bloc-d" font-size="13">count and FLOPs — which is what makes the Table 2 comparison fair.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>
</div>

- The layers fit the <span class="term" data-tiphead="Residual function" data-tip="Instead of asking a stack of layers for the mapping H(x) you want, you ask it for F(x) = H(x) - x and add x back afterwards. Doing nothing then means driving F toward zero, which the paper argues is easier for a solver than fitting an identity with nonlinear layers.">residual</span> `F(x) = H(x) - x`: **doing nothing means driving weights toward zero**, and the block **approaches** an identity
- Close, not exact: each BN ends with a learned per-channel **scale and shift**, so zero conv weights leave `F` equal to the last BN's shift, not 0; and the outer ReLU keeps `x` only because `x` is a ReLU output, never negative
- Why it should be easier — **preconditioning**, recasting a problem so the solver starts nearer the answer: if the best mapping is **closer to identity than to zero**, a **small perturbation of identity** is easier to find than an <span class="term" data-tiphead="Identity mapping" data-tip="A path that returns its input unchanged. On the shortcut it means the block input is simply copied forward: no weights, no gate, no multiplications.">identity mapping</span> rebuilt from conv, BN and ReLU. **Argued, not tested**: no run starts from the identity solution; Figure 7 is the only support ([slide 19](#19))

## Equation 1, term by term, with the shapes written out

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.4rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="980" height="507" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">

<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="40" y="36" class="form-t" font-size="17">Equation 1 has three parts, and the one that does no work is the one that matters</text>
<text x="1120" y="36" text-anchor="end" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="14" font-weight="700">Sec 3.2, Eqn (1)</text>
<g data-tiphead="Block output y" data-tip="The output vector of the layers considered. It has the same shape as x, which is what lets these blocks be stacked without any glue between them.">
<text x="379" y="120" class="form-m" fill="#3fb950" font-size="38" font-weight="700">y</text>
<path d="M379,132 L402,132" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="3" fill="none"/>
</g>
<text x="419" y="120" class="form-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="38">=</text>
<g data-tiphead="Residual mapping F" data-tip="The function the stacked layers actually have to learn. The paper defines it as F(x) := H(x) - x, where H is the mapping you originally wanted.">
<text x="464" y="120" class="form-m" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="38" font-weight="700">F(x, {Wi})</text>
<path d="M464,132 L692,132" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="3" fill="none"/>
</g>
<text x="714" y="120" class="form-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="38">+</text>
<g data-tiphead="The shortcut term x" data-tip="The block input itself, added back element-wise. It is not transformed, not gated and not scaled, which is why it costs nothing.">
<text x="759" y="120" class="form-m" fill="#f0883e" font-size="38" font-weight="700">x</text>
<path d="M759,132 L782,132" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="3" fill="none"/>
</g>
<path d="M390,136 L390,164 L220,164 L220,186" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/>
<path d="M578,136 L578,164 L600,164 L600,186" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/>
<path d="M770,136 L770,164 L960,164 L960,186" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/>
<g data-tiphead="Shape of y" data-tip="Because y must have the same shape as x, a stack of these blocks keeps one width and one map size all the way through a stage: a run of blocks at one feature-map size, conv2_x to conv5_x in Table 1.">
<rect x="40" y="188" width="360" height="128" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a4a66" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="62" y="218" fill="#3fb950" font-size="14.5" font-weight="700">y — what comes out</text>
<text x="62" y="246" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">The sum, before the outer ReLU: ReLU(y) exits.</text>
<text x="62" y="270" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">Same shape as x, so blocks stack directly.</text>
<text x="62" y="294" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">One block, not the whole network.</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="What F contains" data-tip="F can be two or three layers. With one layer only, the paper notes the block is similar to a plain linear layer and it observed no advantage.">
<rect x="420" y="188" width="360" height="128" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="442" y="218" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="14.5" font-weight="700">F — where every weight lives</text>
<text x="442" y="246" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">Two layers here: F = W2 . ReLU(W1 x), with</text>
<text x="442" y="270" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">the biases omitted to simplify notation.</text>
<text x="442" y="294" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">The Wi are the block's learnable weights.</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="Why the identity path is free" data-tip="There is no matrix on this path. Nothing is learned, nothing is multiplied, so the shortcut adds neither extra parameter nor computation complexity.">
<rect x="800" y="188" width="320" height="128" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#4a3520" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="822" y="218" fill="#f0883e" font-size="14.5" font-weight="700">x — carried, not computed</text>
<text x="822" y="246" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">The input itself, unchanged. No matrix,</text>
<text x="822" y="270" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">no gate, never closed. Hence zero extra</text>
<text x="822" y="294" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">parameters and zero extra multiplies.</text>
</g>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S3.SS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="The addition is element-wise" data-tip="Performed on two feature maps channel by channel. Every entry of F(x) is added to the entry of x at the same position and channel, so the two tensors must have identical shape.">
<rect x="40" y="344" width="530" height="236" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="64" y="378" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15.5" font-weight="700">Walking one block, shape by shape</text>
<text x="64" y="404" class="form-d" font-size="13">block input x</text>
<text x="530" y="404" text-anchor="end" class="form-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="13">56 x 56 x 64</text>
<text x="64" y="428" class="form-d" font-size="13">after the first 3x3, 64</text>
<text x="530" y="428" text-anchor="end" class="form-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="13">56 x 56 x 64</text>
<text x="64" y="452" class="form-d" font-size="13">after the second 3x3, 64 — this is F(x)</text>
<text x="530" y="452" text-anchor="end" class="form-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="13">56 x 56 x 64</text>
<text x="64" y="476" class="form-d" font-size="13">the shortcut hands back x, untouched</text>
<text x="530" y="476" text-anchor="end" class="form-m" fill="#f0883e" font-size="13">56 x 56 x 64</text>
<text x="64" y="500" class="form-d" font-size="13">F(x) + x, one add per entry</text>
<text x="530" y="500" text-anchor="end" class="form-m" fill="#3fb950" font-size="13">56 x 56 x 64</text>
<text x="64" y="530" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">Weights on the shortcut: none. Multiplies on the shortcut: none.</text>
<text x="64" y="552" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">Shapes follow Table 1, conv2_x of the 34-layer net.</text>
<text x="64" y="572" class="form-d" font-size="12.5">224x224 input, halved by the stride-2 conv1 and by max pooling.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S3.SS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Equation 2, the mismatch case" data-tip="At a stage boundary the channel count doubles and the feature map halves, so x and F(x) no longer have the same shape and cannot be added. Equation 2 inserts a linear projection Ws on the shortcut, done by 1x1 convolutions with a stride of 2.">
<rect x="590" y="344" width="530" height="236" rx="12" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="614" y="378" class="form-t" font-size="15.5">When the shapes do not match</text>
<text x="855" y="424" text-anchor="middle" class="form-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="26">y = F(x, {Wi}) + Ws x</text>
<text x="1096" y="452" text-anchor="end" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700">Eqn (2)</text>
<text x="614" y="482" class="form-d" font-size="13">Eqn (1) needs x and F(x) the same shape. At each stage</text>
<text x="614" y="506" class="form-d" font-size="13">boundary both change: channels double and the map halves,</text>
<text x="614" y="530" class="form-d" font-size="13">56x56x64 → 28x28x128. Ws is then a 1x1 conv with stride 2.</text>
<text x="614" y="560" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">The paper: Ws is only used when matching dimensions.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>

## Three ways to cross a stage boundary — and the best number is not the one that ships <span class="finfo" data-tiphead="Figure forensics" data-tip="Table 3 is 10-crop testing on the ImageNet validation set, reported without repeats or error bars. A, B and C are separated by fractions of a point — a margin the paper reads as showing projections are not essential, which is why it decides on cost. Option A is what Table 2 and every CIFAR model use; option B is what ResNet-50/101/152 ship with. Table 4 lists the same ResNet-34 B at 21.84 top-1: that is multi-scale testing, not a better model.">ⓘ forensics</span>

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.4rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="980" height="507" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">

<text x="40" y="34" class="shor-t" font-size="17">One stage boundary, three wirings — measured on ResNet-34 with everything else held fixed</text>
<g data-tiphead="Option A — zero-padded identity" data-tip="The shortcut still performs identity mapping, with extra zero entries padded for increasing dimensions, and across the stage boundary it is performed with a stride of 2. <text x="64" y="86" class="shor-t" font-size="16">A — pad with zeros</text>
<text x="64" y="108" class="shor-d" font-size="12.5">parameter-free everywhere</text>
<circle cx="175" cy="288" r="19" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="175" y="295" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="19" font-weight="700">+</text>
<text x="175" y="326" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3fb950" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700">28x28x128 out</text>
<text x="64" y="352" class="shor-d" font-size="12.5">Identity at stride 2 keeps every other</text>

<rect x="40" y="464" width="1080" height="122" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="66" y="492" class="shor-t" font-size="15.5">C scores best and B wins the paper — because the deciding criterion is cost, not accuracy</text>
<text x="66" y="518" class="shor-d" font-size="13">All three beat plain-34 by a wide margin. B is slightly better than A — the paper argues because the zero-padded channels in A do no residual learning;</text>
<text x="66" y="542" class="shor-d" font-size="13">C is only marginally better than B, which the paper puts down to the extra parameters in its thirteen projection shortcuts. ResNet-50/101/152 use B.</text>
<text x="66" y="568" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">Reported without repeats or error bars, these gaps are 0.33 to 0.84 points of top-1: the ranking A, B, C is suggestive, not established.</text>

## One more layer and 4x the width, at the two-layer block's price

<div class="figxs">
<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.2rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="860" height="445" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">

<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="40" y="34" class="bott-t" font-size="17">Figure 5, both blocks, with the multiply-adds written out underneath</text>

<text x="64" y="103" class="bott-d" font-size="12.5">Figure 5, left. The width the 3x3 sees is the width between blocks.</text>

<circle cx="305" cy="286" r="18" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="305" y="293" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="18" font-weight="700">+</text>
<text x="305" y="336" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3fb950" font-size="13" font-weight="700">out: 64-d</text>
</g>

</g>

<rect x="590" y="50" width="530" height="312" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="614" y="82" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15.5" font-weight="700">Bottleneck block — ResNet-50/101/152</text>
<text x="614" y="103" class="bott-d" font-size="12.5">Figure 5, right. The 3x3 sees a quarter of the width between blocks.</text>

</g>

</g>

<text x="800" y="285" text-anchor="middle" class="bott-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="14">1x1, 256</text>
</g>

<path d="M800,184 L800,196" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#ng)"/>
<path d="M800,244 L800,256" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#ng)"/>
<path d="M800,304 L800,308" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#ng)"/>
<path d="M800,132 L660,132 L660,330 L778,330" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#nb)"/>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S4.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="The arithmetic behind similar time complexity" data-tip="Counting multiply-adds per output position: a 3x3 convolution costs 9 times in-channels times out-channels, a 1x1 convolution costs in-channels times out-channels. Squeezing the 3x3 down to 64 channels is what keeps the three-layer block affordable. The paper prints only the shapes and the phrase similar time complexity; the products in the right-hand column were multiplied out for this deck so the claim can be checked rather than taken on trust.">
<rect x="40" y="376" width="1080" height="212" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="66" y="406" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15.5" font-weight="700">The arithmetic, in multiply-adds per output position</text>
<text x="66" y="434" fill="#7a7a7a" font-size="12.5">a 3x3 conv costs 9 x in x out; a 1x1 conv costs in x out</text>
<text x="1094" y="434" text-anchor="end" fill="#d29922" font-size="12.5">totals derived for this deck — the paper prints the shapes, not the products</text>
<text x="66" y="462" class="bott-d" font-size="13.5">two 3x3 layers at 64 channels</text>
<text x="936" y="462" text-anchor="end" class="bott-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="14">2 x 9 x 64 x 64</text>
<text x="1094" y="462" text-anchor="end" class="bott-m" fill="#d29922" font-size="14">= 73,728</text>
<text x="66" y="490" class="bott-d" font-size="13.5">bottleneck: 1x1 down, 3x3 narrow, 1x1 back up</text>
<text x="936" y="490" text-anchor="end" class="bott-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="14">256 x 64 + 9 x 64 x 64 + 64 x 256</text>
<text x="1094" y="490" text-anchor="end" class="bott-m" fill="#d29922" font-size="14">= 69,632</text>
<text x="66" y="518" class="bott-d" font-size="13.5">the same 3x3 pair run straight on 256 channels</text>
<text x="936" y="518" text-anchor="end" class="bott-m" fill="#f85149" font-size="14">2 x 9 x 256 x 256</text>
<text x="1094" y="518" text-anchor="end" class="bott-m" fill="#f85149" font-size="14">= 1,179,648</text>
<text x="66" y="550" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13.5">73,728 against 69,632 — the three-layer block is the cheaper of the two. That is the paper's both designs have similar time complexity.</text>
<text x="66" y="574" class="bott-d" font-size="13.5">1,179,648 is what the two-layer design would cost at the bottleneck's 256-d width — 16x the first line. The 1x1 pair avoids exactly that.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>
</div>

- A <span class="term" data-tiphead="Bottleneck block" data-tip="A three-layer block of 1x1, 3x3, 1x1 convolutions. The 1x1 layers reduce and then restore the channel count so that the expensive 3x3 convolution runs on a narrower tensor.">bottleneck</span> is `1x1 → 3x3 → 1x1`. Figure 5 holds the **56x56 map and the 64-channel 3x3 fixed**; the bottleneck adds a layer and carries **4x the width, 256 channels, between blocks**
- ResNet-50 swaps each of ResNet-34's **16** two-layer blocks for one: 16 × 3 + 2 = **50** layers, the +2 being the first 7x7 conv and the final fc layer. 101 and 152 stack more blocks per stage — **3-4-23-3** and **3-8-36-3** (Table 1)
- Cost: **3.8 / 7.6 / 11.3 billion** <span class="term" data-tiphead="FLOPs" data-tip="Floating point operations for one forward pass on one image, counted here as multiply-adds. It is a proxy for compute cost, not a measured runtime.">FLOPs</span> against VGG-19's **19.6 billion**

## Identity is load-bearing here: a projection would sit on the two widest points of the block

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.4rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="980" height="507" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.bott-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.bott-m{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace}.bott-d{fill:#a0a0a0}</style>
<defs>
<marker id="ig" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L8,3.5 L0,7 z" fill="#3b82f6"/></marker>
<marker id="ib" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L8,3.5 L0,7 z" fill="#3fb950"/></marker>
<marker id="ir" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L8,3.5 L0,7 z" fill="#f85149"/></marker>
</defs>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="40" y="34" class="bott-t" font-size="17">The same bottleneck twice, differing only in what sits on the shortcut</text>
<g data-tiphead="Identity on a bottleneck shortcut" data-tip="The shortcut joins the 256-channel input to the 256-channel output. Left as identity it holds no weights at all, so the block costs exactly its three convolutions.">
<rect x="40" y="50" width="530" height="330" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="64" y="82" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15.5" font-weight="700">Identity shortcut — what the paper builds within a stage</text>
<text x="305" y="112" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3fb950" font-size="13" font-weight="700">256-d</text>
<circle cx="305" cy="298" r="18" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="305" y="305" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="18" font-weight="700">+</text>
<text x="305" y="344" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3fb950" font-size="13" font-weight="700">256-d</text>
<text x="64" y="364" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="13">weights on the shortcut: none — multiplies on the shortcut: none</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="1x1 down-projection" data-tip="Cuts the 256 incoming channels to 64 before the expensive 3x3 runs.">
<rect x="215" y="124" width="180" height="38" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="305" y="148" text-anchor="middle" class="bott-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13.5">1x1, 64</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="The bottleneck 3x3" data-tip="The expensive layer, running on the narrow 64-channel tensor.">
<rect x="215" y="174" width="180" height="38" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="305" y="198" text-anchor="middle" class="bott-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13.5">3x3, 64</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="1x1 up-projection" data-tip="Restores the width to 256 so the branch output matches what the shortcut is carrying.">
<rect x="215" y="224" width="180" height="38" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>

<text x="1094" y="518" text-anchor="end" class="bott-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="14">64 x 64</text>
<text x="66" y="550" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13.5">The middle line is nearly the whole first line again. The paper: the time complexity and model size are doubled, as the shortcut is</text>
<text x="66" y="572" class="bott-d" font-size="13.5">connected to the two high-dimensional ends. On a two-layer block the same choice is sixteen times cheaper and nobody would notice.</text>
</a>

## The paper's own Figure 4: the same two depths, plain on the left, shortcuts added on the right

<p style="text-align:center; margin:0"><span style="position:relative; display:inline-block"><img src="images/paper/fig4-imagenet-curves.png" width="940" style="border-radius:6px"/><span class="hotspot" data-tiphead="Left — plain-18 vs plain-34" data-tip="ImageNet training. - **plain-34 is worse than plain-18; ResNet-34 is better than ResNet-18** — same depth, same width, same parameter count on both sides. Scope: option A, 18 and 34 layers; for bottleneck nets only a footnote says plain twins degrade too, with no numbers
- At 18 layers the two are a tie: when the net is *not overly deep* SGD still finds good plain solutions, and the ResNet only **converges faster** — the paper's reading of Figure 4, *at the early stage*, with no number given
- One run per network, no error bars: trust rests on the **size and direction** of the gaps, and on CIFAR-10 repeating them (paper's Figure 6: plain worse from 20 to 56 layers, ResNets better)

## The paper spends a paragraph ruling out the answer everyone gives

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.2rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="860" height="445" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.notv-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.notv-m{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace}.notv-d{fill:#a0a0a0}.notv-b{fill:#f0f0f0;font-size:12}</style>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="40" y="32" class="notv-t" font-size="17">Four independent observations, all pointing away from the same explanation</text>
<g data-tiphead="The claim being ruled out" data-tip="The paper argues this optimization difficulty is unlikely to be caused by vanishing gradients, and gives four separate reasons. Vanishing gradients were the obstacle before this paper, and the introduction says they had been largely addressed by normalized initialization and intermediate normalization layers.">
<rect x="40" y="48" width="1080" height="76" rx="12" fill="#1a1113" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="66" y="82" fill="#f85149" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700">THE ANSWER MOST PEOPLE GIVE</text>
<text x="66" y="108" fill="#c8c8c8" font-size="18">Deep plain nets fail because the gradient vanishes on the way back, and the shortcut gives it a highway</text>
<path d="M62,101 L1004,101" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="2.4"/>
<text x="1094" y="86" text-anchor="end" fill="#f85149" font-size="13" font-weight="700">the paper: unlikely</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="Batch normalisation is already there" data-tip="Section 3.4: batch normalisation is adopted right after each convolution and before activation, in the plain networks as well as the residual ones. That is what keeps the forward signal alive.">
<rect x="40" y="144" width="258" height="256" rx="11" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="62" y="176" class="notv-t" font-size="13.5">1. BN is already everywhere</text>
<text x="62" y="206" class="notv-b">BN sits right after every</text>
<text x="62" y="226" class="notv-b">convolution and before the</text>
<text x="62" y="246" class="notv-b">activation — in the plain</text>
<text x="62" y="266" class="notv-b">networks too, not only the</text>
<text x="62" y="286" class="notv-b">residual ones.</text>
<path d="M62,308 L276,308" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<text x="62" y="334" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5">which ensures forward</text>
<text x="62" y="354" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5">propagated signals to have</text>
<text x="62" y="374" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5">non-zero variances</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="The gradients were checked" data-tip="Section 4.1, in one sentence: the authors verify that the backward propagated gradients exhibit healthy norms with BN, and conclude that neither forward nor backward signals vanish. No plot, number or definition of healthy is given, so this is the weakest of the four observations.">
<rect x="314" y="144" width="258" height="256" rx="11" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="336" y="176" class="notv-t" font-size="13.5">2. They say they looked</text>
<text x="336" y="206" class="notv-b">One sentence in Section 4.1:</text>
<text x="336" y="226" class="notv-b">the backward gradients were</text>
<text x="336" y="246" class="notv-b">checked and found healthy.</text>
<text x="336" y="266" class="notv-b">No plot, number or definition</text>
<text x="336" y="286" fill="#f0883e" font-size="12">— the weakest of the four.</text>
<path d="M336,308 L550,308" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<text x="336" y="334" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5">gradients exhibit healthy</text>
<text x="336" y="354" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5">norms, so neither forward</text>
<text x="336" y="374" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5">nor backward signals vanish</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="The plain net is not dead" data-tip="A network whose gradients had vanished would not learn at all. plain-34 reaches accuracy in the same range as VGG-16, which the paper reads as the solver working to some extent.">
<rect x="588" y="144" width="258" height="256" rx="11" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="610" y="176" class="notv-t" font-size="13.5">3. plain-34 still learns</text>
<text x="610" y="206" class="notv-b">A net with dead gradients</text>
<text x="610" y="226" class="notv-b">would not train at all. This</text>
<text x="610" y="246" class="notv-b">one reaches competitive</text>
<text x="610" y="266" class="notv-b">accuracy — it is worse than</text>
<text x="610" y="286" class="notv-b">plain-18, not broken.</text>
<path d="M610,308 L824,308" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<text x="610" y="334" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5">Table 3, top-1 / top-5, 10-crop</text>
<text x="610" y="358" class="notv-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13.5">plain-34: 28.54 / 10.02</text>
<text x="610" y="380" class="notv-m" fill="#a0a0a0" font-size="13.5">VGG-16: 28.07 / 9.33</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="It is not impatience either" data-tip="Footnote 3: the authors experimented with three times more training iterations and still observed the degradation problem, so it cannot feasibly be addressed by simply training for longer.">
<rect x="862" y="144" width="258" height="256" rx="11" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="884" y="176" class="notv-t" font-size="13.5">4. Not a patience problem</text>
<text x="884" y="206" class="notv-b">Footnote 3 reports running</text>
<text x="884" y="226" class="notv-b">the same experiment with</text>
<text x="884" y="246" class="notv-b">three times the iterations.</text>
<text x="884" y="266" class="notv-b">The degradation was still</text>
<text x="884" y="286" class="notv-b">there at the end.</text>
<path d="M884,308 L1098,308" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<text x="884" y="334" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5">this problem cannot be</text>
<text x="884" y="354" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5">feasibly addressed by simply</text>
<text x="884" y="374" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5">using more iterations</text>
</g>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S4.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="What the paper offers instead" data-tip="Section 4.1 ends with a conjecture, not an explanation: the deep plain nets may have exponentially low convergence rates, which impact the reducing of the training error. The reason for such optimization difficulties will be studied in the future.">
<rect x="40" y="422" width="1080" height="164" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="66" y="454" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15.5" font-weight="700">So what does the paper put in its place? A conjecture, and an open question</text>
<text x="66" y="482" class="notv-d" font-size="13.5">It conjectures that the deep plain nets may have exponentially low convergence rates, which impact the reducing of the training error,</text>
<text x="66" y="504" class="notv-d" font-size="13.5">and then says plainly that the reason for such optimization difficulties will be studied in the future.</text>
<text x="66" y="527" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="13">Read the conjecture as: training error keeps falling, but so slowly that no feasible schedule reaches the shallower net — footnote 3 tried 3x the iterations.</text>
<text x="66" y="554" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13.5">Worth being blunt about: this paper demonstrates that residual learning fixes degradation. It does not explain why degradation</text>
<text x="66" y="575" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13.5">happens, and it explicitly declines the explanation almost everyone repeats.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>

- <span class="term" data-tiphead="Batch normalisation" data-tip="Normalises each channel over the current mini-batch to zero mean and unit variance, then rescales with learned parameters. Here it is applied right after every convolution and before the activation.">Batch normalisation</span> is applied after **every** convolution in the plain nets too, so the forward signal is demonstrably alive
- What replaces the explanation is a **conjecture** — <span class="term" data-tiphead="Exponentially low convergence rates" data-tip="The paper's phrase, not defined further. One plain reading: the training error keeps falling, but so slowly that no feasible schedule reaches the shallower net's error. Footnote 3 fits that reading: three times the iterations still left the degradation in place.">exponentially low convergence rates</span> — and an admission that the reason is still open. The paper does not say exponential in what. Longer training closing the gap would undercut it; 3x the iterations did not (footnote 3) — consistent, not proof

## Easier to fit the residual is a hypothesis with a correlation behind it, not a result

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.4rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="980" height="507" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.resp-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.resp-d{fill:#a0a0a0}.resp-ax{fill:#6e6e6e;font-size:11.5}</style>

<text x="40" y="34" class="resp-t" font-size="17">Every layer of a ResNet moves the signal less than its plain equivalent does</text>

<text x="82" y="191" text-anchor="end" class="resp-ax">2</text>
<text x="82" y="287" text-anchor="end" class="resp-ax">1</text>
<text x="82" y="384" text-anchor="end" class="resp-ax">0</text>
<text x="90" y="398" class="resp-ax">0</text>
<text x="368" y="398" text-anchor="middle" class="resp-ax">60</text>
<text x="600" y="398" text-anchor="middle" class="resp-ax">110</text>

<g data-tiphead="plain-20 and plain-56" data-tip="The two plain networks sit highest: every layer changes the signal by a lot. Residual nets sit visibly below them at the same depth.">
<path d="M90,129 L109,177 L127,206 L146,235 L164,264 L183,293" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none"/>

</g>
<text x="90" y="444" fill="#f0883e" font-size="12" font-weight="700">plain-20</text>
<text x="180" y="444" fill="#f85149" font-size="12" font-weight="700">plain-56</text>
<text x="270" y="444" fill="#3fb950" font-size="12" font-weight="700">ResNet-20</text>
<text x="372" y="444" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12" font-weight="700">ResNet-56</text>
<text x="474" y="444" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="12" font-weight="700">ResNet-110</text>
<text x="90" y="470" class="resp-ax">Redrawn from Figure 7, lower panel; curve shapes schematic.</text>
<rect x="60" y="490" width="560" height="92" rx="12" fill="#151515" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="84" y="518" fill="#f0883e" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700">VERDICT: LITTLE WEIGHT ON ITS OWN</text>
<text x="84" y="542" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">Figure 7 shows the pattern the hypothesis predicts, but nothing</text>
<text x="84" y="564" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">rules out other causes. A consistency check, not a test.</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1512.03385#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Hypothesis, support, and the gap between them" data-tip="Section 3.1 states the intuition as a hypothesis and Section 4.2 offers the response magnitudes as support. The paper never claims to have isolated the mechanism.">
<rect x="640" y="52" width="480" height="374" rx="12" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="664" y="86" class="resp-t" font-size="15.5">Argument by construction, evidence by correlation</text>
<text x="664" y="114" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700">THE HYPOTHESIS, SEC 3.1</text>
<text x="664" y="136" class="resp-d" font-size="13">The authors hypothesize that it is easier to optimize the</text>
<text x="664" y="156" class="resp-d" font-size="13">residual mapping than the original, unreferenced mapping.</text>
<text x="664" y="184" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700">THE SUPPORT, SEC 4.2</text>
<text x="664" y="206" class="resp-d" font-size="13">In a ResNet, the second layer's response is F(x) itself.</text>
<text x="664" y="226" class="resp-d" font-size="13">ResNets have generally smaller responses than their plain</text>
<text x="664" y="246" class="resp-d" font-size="13">counterparts, and deeper ResNets smaller still. The chain:</text>
<text x="664" y="266" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="13">small std of F(x) → F changes x little → near identity.</text>
<text x="664" y="294" fill="#f0883e" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700">WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH</text>
<text x="664" y="316" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="12.5">There is no ablation in the paper that turns the mechanism off.</text>
<text x="664" y="338" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">BN's learned scale sets each std directly, so a small</text>
<text x="664" y="358" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">response is the solver picking a small scale: consistent</text>
<text x="664" y="378" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">with the hypothesis, not proof of it. The paper's own</text>
<text x="664" y="398" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13">wording is hedged: hypothesize, then might.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.06431" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Where the explanation went afterwards" data-tip="Veit, Wilber and Belongie argued a ResNet behaves like an ensemble of relatively shallow networks; Balduzzi et al. described shattered gradients in plain nets; Li et al. visualised skip connections smoothing the loss landscape. All of them postdate this paper.">
<rect x="640" y="448" width="480" height="134" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="664" y="480" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="14.5" font-weight="700">The result held; the explanation did not settle</text>
<text x="664" y="508" class="resp-d" font-size="13">Later accounts attribute the gain to ensembles of shallow</text>
<text x="664" y="530" class="resp-d" font-size="13">paths, to gradients staying correlated rather than shattering,</text>
<text x="664" y="552" class="resp-d" font-size="13">and to a smoother loss landscape. Slide 23 lists them with</text>
<text x="664" y="574" class="resp-d" font-size="13">links; none of them existed when this paper was written.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>

- **3.57%** is six models combined, scored on the **test** set by the evaluation server; **4.49%** is the best single model, on **validation**
- Tables 2 and 3 are neither: they use <span class="term" data-tiphead="10-crop testing" data-tip="The score for an image is averaged over ten fixed crops: the four corners, the centre, and the horizontal flips of all five. It is a mild test-time ensemble, so its numbers are not comparable to single-crop ones.">10-crop testing</span> for like-for-like comparison rather than for the headline

## At 1202 layers it trains beautifully and generalises worse — and the authors say so first <span class="finfo" data-tiphead="Figure forensics" data-tip="ResNet-110 is the only configuration in the paper that is repeated: five runs, reported as best 6.43 with mean 6.61 plus or minus 0.16. The 1202-layer row is a single reported number, so 6.43 against 7.93 sets one run against the best of five. The paper's own reading is overfitting on a small dataset, and it notes no regularisation such as maxout or dropout was applied.">ⓘ forensics</span>

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.2rem">

<text x="40" y="34" class="cifa-t" font-size="17">CIFAR-10 is where the paper pushes depth until it stops paying</text>
<text x="90" y="66" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="13.5" font-weight="700">CIFAR-10, ResNets of 110 and 1202 layers</text>

<path d="M98,90 L132,181 L175,220 L218,233 L260,242 L302,249 L345,254 L362,304 L430,318 L498,321 L515,342 L600,346" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>

- Same [Faster R-CNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.01497) code, same proposal setup, same hyper-parameters: the paper argues the gain is **solely due to the learned representations**
- **Verdict:** a better backbone transfers; the swap is the **backbone as a whole**, not the shortcut — ResNet-101 is also deeper, cheaper (**7.6 vs 15.3 billion FLOPs**) and attached differently, via <span class="term" data-tiphead="Networks on Conv feature maps (NoC)" data-tip="ResNet has no hidden fully-connected layers to act as the per-region head. So conv1 to conv4_x, 91 conv layers, compute the shared feature maps at a stride of 16 pixels like VGG-16's 13 conv layers, and conv5_x runs on each region after RoI pooling, in the role of VGG-16's fc layers.">NoC</span>; no plain-101 detector is tested
- **mAP** (mean average precision): precision averaged over recall levels and classes, a box counting as correct above 0.5 box overlap (IoU); **mAP@[.5, .95]** averages over ten IoU thresholds, 0.5 to 0.95, so it also rewards tight boxes
- Competition entries built on them won **ImageNet detection, ImageNet localization, [COCO](https://cocodataset.org/) detection and COCO segmentation** at [ILSVRC 2015](https://www.image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/2015/) — five 1st places with classification

<a class="slide-id" id="62fa1249-71d0-4c77-84ee-fc4bc5880534"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## Challenge the assumptions

| claim | status |
|---|---|
| plain nets degrade on **training** error | **holds** — Figures 1 and 4 |
| identity shortcuts reverse it | **holds**, single runs — Table 2 at matched parameter count (option A, 18/34 layers) and Figure 6 on CIFAR-10; bottleneck nets: one footnote, no numbers |
| it is **not** vanishing gradients | **mostly holds** — BN throughout; the gradient-norm check is one sentence, no plot |
| residuals are intrinsically easier to fit | **contested** — Figure 7 is a correlation; [ensembles](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.06431) · [shattered gradients](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08591) · [loss surface](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.09913) |
| ReLU belongs after the addition | **revised** — [pre-activation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.05027), same authors |
| depth always pays | **bounded on CIFAR-10** — one 1202-layer run overfits |

- **Single runs, no error bars** — only CIFAR ResNet-110 is repeated (6.43 best, 6.61 ± 0.16); the ImageNet A/B/C margins come with no spread at all.

---

<a class="slide-id" id="20be3a17-15cd-4f97-be5b-dc02a2299b24"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## Steal list — three habits worth copying, and the gap each one closes

- **Split "worse" into training-worse and test-worse** — the paper turns on it *(effort: free)*.
  <span class="ev">A report with a single eval metric makes deeper-is-worse look like overfitting.</span>
- **The construction argument as a debugging tool** — if the bigger model reproduces the smaller one exactly, failing to match it is an **optimisation bug, not a capacity limit** *(effort: hours)*.
  <span class="ev">A recipe, not from the paper: (1) build the bigger model from the smaller one's trained weights, extra blocks set to identity; (2) check it reproduces the smaller model's training loss; (3) train the bigger one from scratch — ending above that loss is an optimisation gap. Rarely a required check before scaling up.</span>
- **Cost-first ablation reading** — the paper takes option B over the better option C, judging a sub-point margin not worth the extra parameters *(effort: free)*.
  <span class="ev">Results tables often bold the best cell without a second seed.</span>

---

<a class="slide-id" id="5c2e8f1a-3b7d-4e9a-a6c4-7d1f0b2e9a51"></a>

## What to keep from this paper

- **When a deeper model is worse, compare training error before anything else** — higher training error means an optimisation problem, and regularisation will not fix it.
- **Build new layers so that doing nothing is the easy default** — wrap them in an identity shortcut, so added depth starts close to the shallower net.
- **Keep shortcuts identity and project only where the shape changes** — in bottleneck blocks a projection on every shortcut would double cost and model size.
- **Quote every number with its protocol** — split, single model or ensemble, crops, top-1 or top-5: the same ResNet-34 B is 24.52 or 21.84 top-1 depending on testing alone.
- **A default for today — later practice, not this paper:** bottleneck blocks with identity shortcuts, a projection only between stages, and the last BN scale in each block initialised to zero so every block starts as an identity ([Goyal et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02677)); for very deep stacks, [pre-activation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.05027) ordering keeps the shortcut a pure identity.

**If you do one thing:** when a bigger model is worse, check its training error before reaching for regularisation.

---

<a class="slide-id" id="151bc713-0cb4-4f1a-9df3-9df9c0e337a7"></a>

## Discussion — open questions for the group

<div class="dq">

**The mechanism is still contested — does that change how skips should be used?**
<span class="ev">If ResNets work as ensembles of shallow paths, depth budgets, pruning and early-exit designs all change.</span>

</div>

<div class="dq">

**On CIFAR-10, one 1202-layer run did worse than 110 layers — overfitting, the paper argues. Where does depth stop paying on a given dataset?**
<span class="ev">The best tested depth there was 110 layers. For a new dataset the crossover is unknown until measured.</span>

</div>

<div class="dq">

**A, B and C differ by a fraction of a point. How many published ablation wins sit inside a margin like that?**
<span class="ev">The paper read a sub-point margin as projections being non-essential and picked on cost.</span>

</div>

## Appendix — figure hover notes 1/7: the task, the result, and the two failure modes (reviewable record)

| on | element | what the hover says |
|---|---|---|
| [s4](#4) | **Figure 2 — the building block** | The paper's own drawing of one residual block: two weight layers compute F(x), the curved identity path carries x around them, and the two are added before the final ReLU. Slide 11 redraws it piece by piece. |
| [s3](#3) | **The input** | One RGB image, a 224x224 crop. The models are trained on the 1.28 million ImageNet training images and evaluated on the 50k validation images; the final headline number comes from the 100k test images and is reported by the test server. |
| [s3](#3) | **The network** | ResNet-152: 152 layers, 11.3 billion FLOPs. The paper's framing is that this is 8 times deeper than VGG nets and still has lower complexity than VGG-16/19, which cost 15.3 and 19.6 billion FLOPs. Depth is cheap here because the layers are narrow and most 3x3 convolutions run inside bottleneck blocks at a quarter of the width, slide 14. |
| [s3](#3) | **The output** | A score for every one of the 1000 ImageNet classes. Top-1 error counts an image as wrong when the highest-scoring class is not the truth; top-5 error counts it as wrong only when the truth is outside the five highest-scoring classes. Lower is better in both cases. |
| [s3](#3) | **The headline bar** | 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set, from an ensemble of six models of different depth — only two of them 152-layer at the time of submission. This entry won 1st place in ILSVRC 2015. It is not a single-model number. |
| [s3](#3) | **Two protocols in one chart** | The 4.49% row is a single model scored on the 50k validation images. The other rows are test-set numbers reported by the evaluation server on the 100k test images. The paper reports both, and mixing them is the easiest mistake to make with this paper. |
| [s7](#7) | **Left panel — training error** | Training error on CIFAR-10 for two plain networks. The red 56-layer curve stays above the yellow 20-layer curve for the entire run, so the deeper net fits the data it is optimised on worse. This panel alone rules out overfitting. |
| [s7](#7) | **Right panel — test error** | Test error for the same two runs. The ordering is unchanged: 56 layers above 20 layers. The paper's caption reads the right panel as a consequence of the left one: higher training error, and thus test error. |
| [s8](#8) | **20-layer plain net, training error** | The shallower of the two. Its training error falls to the bottom of the panel: the solver fits this network well. |
| [s8](#8) | **56-layer plain net, training error** | Nearly three times deeper and it never catches up. Its training error stays above the 20-layer curve for the whole run, so the extra capacity buys nothing. |
| [s8](#8) | **20-layer plain net, test error** | Test error is higher than training error, as always. What matters is that the ordering between the two depths is the same in both panels. |
| [s8](#8) | **56-layer plain net, test error** | The paper's caption: the deeper network has higher training error, and thus test error. Test error is the consequence here, not the diagnosis. |
| [s8](#8) | **The gap, in order** | The 20-layer curve lights up first, then the 56-layer curve settles above it, then the test panel repeats the ordering. The curve shapes are schematic; the ordering is the paper's. |
| [s8](#8) | **Why this is not overfitting** | Overfitting means the model fits the training set too well and the test set worse. Here the deeper model fits the training set worse. Nothing about capacity or regularisation can explain a higher training error. |
| [s9](#9) | **Overfitting** | The model memorises the training set. Training error keeps falling, held-out error turns back up, and the gap between them widens. This is the failure ResNet is NOT about. |
| [s9](#9) | **Vanishing or exploding gradients** | The signal dies on its way through the stack and the network never starts converging. The paper's introduction says this had been largely addressed by normalized initialization and intermediate normalization layers. |
| [s9](#9) | **Degradation** | The network converges perfectly happily, and still lands at a higher training error than a shallower version of itself. This is the failure the paper isolates and the one residual learning is aimed at. |

## Appendix — figure hover notes 2/7: the constructed solution (reviewable record)

| on | element | what the hover says |
|---|---|---|
| [s10](#10) | **A trained shallower network** | Take any network that has already been trained to some training error. Call that error E. |
| [s10](#10) | **A trained shallower network** | Nothing special about these layers: they are whatever the shallower model happened to converge to. |
| [s10](#10) | **A trained shallower network** | The stack is drawn with three layers only for the picture; the argument holds for any depth. |
| [s10](#10) | **The copied layers** | The first layers of the deeper model are copied verbatim from the learned shallower model. Nothing is retrained. |
| [s10](#10) | **The copied layers** | Same weights, same order. The deeper model starts out reproducing the shallower model exactly. |
| [s10](#10) | **The copied layers** | This is why the shallower model's solution space is a subspace of the deeper model's solution space. |
| [s10](#10) | **The added layers are identity** | Every extra layer just passes its input through unchanged, so the deeper network computes exactly the same function as the shallower one. |
| [s10](#10) | **The added layers are identity** | Add as many of these as you like. None of them can raise the training error, because none of them changes the output. |
| [s10](#10) | **The added layers are identity** | Fitting an identity mapping with a stack of nonlinear layers is exactly what the paper suspects solvers find hard. One illustrative way to build it: a 3x3 kernel with a single centred 1 for its own channel, BN set to undo its own normalisation, and a ReLU that sees only non-negative inputs because they come from the previous ReLU. |
| [s10](#10) | **The constructed solution** | The paper: there exists a solution by construction to the deeper model, the added layers are identity mapping, and the other layers are copied from the learned shallower model. |
| [s10](#10) | **What experiments find** | The paper: experiments show that our current solvers on hand are unable to find solutions that are comparably good or better than the constructed solution, or unable to do so in feasible time. |
| [s10](#10) | **Why this motivates residual learning** | If the useful thing is hard to reach because it sits near an identity mapping, change the parameterisation so that identity is what you get when the weights are zero. |
